name: Strait of Hormuz
strategic_role: Connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea; the world's most important oil transit chokepoint by volume
alternative_description: Saudi Aramco's 5 million b/d East-West crude pipeline (Abqaiq to Yanbu on the Red Sea) and a UAE pipeline to the Fujairah export terminal in the Gulf of Oman. EIA estimates about 2.6 million b/d of that capacity could actually be available to bypass Hormuz in a disruption, against roughly 20 million b/d of transit.
flow_data_origin: EIA analysis based on Vortexa tanker tracking
source: EIA Today in Energy - Amid regional conflict the Strait of Hormuz remains critical oil chokepoint
notes: Flow quoted verbatim: 'In 2024, oil flow through the strait averaged 20 million barrels per day (b/d), or the equivalent of about 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption.' baseline_oil_flow_mbd stores observed THROUGHPUT (20), not capacity; the 2.6 million b/d and 5 million b/d figures mentioned elsewhere in this row are bypass-PIPELINE capacities and are deliberately NOT stored in the flow column, because capacity and flow are different quantities. flow_data_origin records that the underlying tanker-tracking data is Vortexa, a COMMERCIAL source, published through EIA - it is not an EIA-collected statistic. alternative_exists='partial' because bypass pipelines exist but their usable spare capacity is roughly an eighth of the transit volume. This row records a HISTORICAL BASELINE only; no current risk level is asserted here and none should be inferred.

name: Bab el-Mandeb Strait
strategic_role: Chokepoint between the Horn of Africa and the Middle East connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea; a strategic link between the Mediterranean Sea and the Indian Ocean
alternative_description: Cargoes can be rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope (CP006), which EIA states adds approximately 2,700 miles to the transit from Saudi Arabia to the United States.
flow_data_origin: EIA analysis based on Vortexa data
source: EIA Today in Energy - Fewer tankers transit the Red Sea in 2024
notes: Flow quoted verbatim: 'Oil trade flows through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait averaged 4.0 million barrels per day (b/d) in 2024 through August compared with 8.7 million b/d in full-year 2023, according to Vortexa data.' The 2023 comparator of 8.7 million b/d is recorded here rather than in the numeric column because the column holds ONE period; the drop between the two periods is a documented historical fact, NOT a permanent property of this chokepoint. flow_period is a PARTIAL year (January-August 2024) and must not be compared with full-year figures without adjustment. Underlying data is Vortexa, a commercial source, published through EIA.

name: Suez Canal
strategic_role: Connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Suez with the Mediterranean Sea; a strategic route for Persian Gulf oil and natural gas shipments to Europe and North America
alternative_description: The SUMED pipeline (CP004) is the only alternate route from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean if ships cannot navigate the canal; otherwise cargoes divert around the Cape of Good Hope (CP006).
flow_basis: crude oil and refined products both directions
source: EIA Today in Energy - Three important oil trade chokepoints are located around the Arabian Peninsula
notes: Flow quoted verbatim: 'In 2016, 3.9 million b/d of crude oil and refined products transited the Suez Canal in both directions, according to data published by the Suez Canal Authority.' STALENESS WARNING: this is a 2016 figure published in 2017 and is the most recent Suez Canal figure this project could source as text from an official publisher. It is a historical baseline and is very likely not representative of current flows. Refreshing it is listed as a manual action in docs/phase1_report.md.

name: SUMED Pipeline
strategic_role: Crude oil pipeline transporting crude north through Egypt from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean; the only alternate route to the Suez Canal for Red Sea to Mediterranean movements
alternative_description: The Suez Canal (CP003) is the maritime alternative for the same origin-destination pair.
source: EIA Today in Energy - Three important oil trade chokepoints are located around the Arabian Peninsula
notes: Flow quoted verbatim: 'In 2016, 1.6 million b/d of crude oil was transported through the SUMED Pipeline to the Mediterranean Sea and then loaded onto tankers for seaborne trade.' IMPORTANT: baseline_oil_flow_mbd holds ACTUAL THROUGHPUT (1.6), not capacity. The separately published pipeline CAPACITY is 2.5 million b/d and is deliberately NOT stored in the flow column, because capacity and flow are different quantities. Coordinates are null: SUMED is a linear pipeline, not a point feature, and a single centroid would misrepresent it. STALENESS WARNING: 2016 figure, as for CP003.

name: Strait of Malacca
strategic_role: Connects the Indian Ocean with the Pacific Ocean through the South China Sea between Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore; the shortest sea route between Persian Gulf suppliers and key Asian markets, and the second-largest oil trade chokepoint after Hormuz
alternative_description: EIA describes Malacca as the shortest route between Gulf suppliers and Asian markets but the sources consulted did not state a specific alternative routing, so alternative_exists is 'unknown' rather than asserted.
source: EIA Today in Energy - The Strait of Malacca a key oil trade chokepoint links the Indian and Pacific Oceans
notes: Flow quoted verbatim: 'Petroleum and other liquids transiting the Strait of Malacca increased for the fourth time in the past five years in 2016, reaching 16 million barrels per day (b/d).' STALENESS WARNING: 2016 figure published in 2017; this is the most recent Malacca figure this project could source as text. EIA has published more recent Malacca commentary but the underlying volumes appear only inside chart images, which this project does not transcribe. Note for Indian modelling: Malacca lies EAST of India and is not on India's Gulf, Red Sea, West African or Atlantic crude import routes; it is relevant to product exports and to regional traffic, not to India's crude inbound corridors.

name: Cape of Good Hope
strategic_role: Sea route around the southern tip of Africa; the principal alternative routing when the Red Sea corridor (Bab el-Mandeb, Suez, SUMED) is avoided
alternative_description: This chokepoint IS the alternative route for CP002, CP003 and CP004. It is an open-ocean rounding rather than a narrow passage, so it cannot be closed in the way a strait or canal can.
flow_data_origin: EIA analysis based on Vortexa data
source: EIA Today in Energy - Fewer tankers transit the Red Sea in 2024
notes: Flow quoted verbatim: 'The volume of crude oil and oil products flowing around the Cape of Good Hope increased to 9.2 million b/d in the first eight months of 2024 from an average of 6.0 million b/d in 2023, according to Vortexa data.' The 2023 comparator of 6.0 million b/d is recorded in this note, not in the numeric column. flow_period is a PARTIAL year (January-August 2024). The rise here and the fall at CP002 over the same period are two sides of the same rerouting; they must not be added together as if independent. Underlying data is Vortexa, a commercial source, published through EIA. Coordinate is the OSM 'Cape of Good Hope' landmark, i.e. the headland, not the shipping lane, which lies further south.

name: Turkish Straits
strategic_role: Key oil export route to Europe for Russia and other Eurasian countries including Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan; comprises the Bosporus and the Dardanelles
alternative_description: No alternative routing was stated in the sources consulted, so alternative_exists is 'unknown' rather than asserted.
source: EIA Today in Energy - Maritime chokepoints are critical to global energy security
notes: baseline_oil_flow_mbd, flow_basis, flow_period and flow_data_origin are ALL NULL: no oil-flow volume for the Turkish Straits was obtainable as text from an official publisher within Phase 1. EIA's figures for this chokepoint appear only inside chart images, which this project does not transcribe into data. This is a documented gap, not a zero - see docs/phase1_report.md. The coordinate given is the Bosporus (Istanbul Strait); the Dardanelles (Canakkale Strait) is the second constriction of the same system at approximately 40.2092, 26.4414, and a single point cannot represent both. EIA notes tanker traffic here faces no specific size restriction but must navigate relatively narrow, difficult sea lanes.
